FlashAccel: Leveraging High-Bandwidth Flash for High-Throughput LLM Inference

Xinyu Wang Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: wangxinyu22s@ict.ac.cn , Yalong Xue Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: School of Advanced Interdisciplinary Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: xueyalong22@mails.ucas.ac.cn , Xiaotian Sun Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: sunxiaotian21s@ict.ac.cn , Xiaoyu Zhang Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: zhangxiaoyu@ict.ac.cn , Chunmeng Dou Affiliation: Institute of Microelectronics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: douchunmeng@ime.ac.cn , Xueqi Li Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: lixueqi@ict.ac.cn and Xiaoming Chen Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China email: chenxiaoming@ict.ac.cn
Abstract.

Large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly limited by the capacity of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in GPUs, as model weights and KV cache grow rapidly. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) provides higher capacity than HBM while retaining comparable bandwidth, making it a promising substrate for capacity-constrained LLM inference. However, its inherently high access latency, low bandwidth utilization, and lack of support for heterogeneous resource management make it difficult to integrate HBF into GPUs for LLM inference. We present FlashAccel, a co-designed system that enables efficient LLM inference using HBF. FlashAccel integrates HBF into HBM-based GPUs, providing architectural support to mitigate access latency. It improves bandwidth utilization through specialized data layouts for both model weights and KV cache, and introduces an HBF-aware storage management layer together with a programming model to organize persistent data in HBF and coordinate heterogeneous memory resources at the system level. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating six HBF stacks into the GPU enables FlashAccel to deliver an average improvement of 2.54×\times and 1.93×\times in throughput per GPU and energy efficiency over the HBM-only GPU under 100ms latency constraint, respectively.

Keywords: 
High Bandwidth Flash, LLM Inference

1. Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) is driving inference workloads toward multi-turn interactions (Deshpande et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2023; Yi et al., 2025), agents (Yao et al., 2022; Park et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023), and long-context processing (Beltagy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2024). Two key trends emerge in this evolution. First, model sizes continue to grow following the scaling law (Kaplan et al., 2020), at the cost of drastically increased parameter scale. Second, new workloads increasingly rely on long context lengths, leading to substantial growth in KV cache footprints during inference (Bhaskar et al., 2025). These trends fundamentally increase the memory capacity requirements of inference systems. However, the capacity of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in GPUs has not kept pace with the rapid growth of model size. Figure 1 shows that, although GPU memory capacity has increased steadily over time, the memory footprint of popular models has grown much faster. Today, models can exceed terabytes in size, far surpassing the capacity of a single GPU, which is at most a few hundred gigabytes. Meanwhile, as the context length has grown by 4×\times on average over the past two years (Aubakirova et al., 2026), the storage overhead of KV cache has increased proportionally by 4×\times.

The limited HBM capacity introduces several critical challenges in LLM inference. First, during the memory-bound decode phase, insufficient memory capacity restricts the batch size, leading to low compute utilization and throughput. Second, the memory pressure often forces early eviction of KV cache, preventing reuse opportunities in multi-turn interactions and increasing recomputation overhead (Kwon et al., 2023). Third, due to the limited capacity of a single GPU, storing large models requires multi-GPU systems, which incur significant hardware cost and introduce additional complexity in inter-GPU communication, task scheduling, and fault tolerance.

Prior works (Yu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025b) have leveraged Flash memories to address the capacity bottleneck. They typically store the model weights in Flash and use in-storage computation to exploit internal parallelism. However, these works are primarily designed for edge scenarios. Their limited bandwidth and computational capacity are insufficient to meet the requirements of high-throughput scenarios that require powerful compute devices (i.e., GPUs) and memory devices with both large capacity and high bandwidth. To provide both high bandwidth and large capacity, High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has been proposed. HBF is a specialized Flash memory that delivers bandwidth comparable to HBM while retaining the high density and non-volatility of Flash (Ha et al., 2026; Hsu et al., 2026). By integrating HBF into the GPU alongside HBM, we can significantly expand memory capacity to achieve potentially higher decode throughput. However, this capacity advantage does not automatically translate into throughput gains.

Several critical challenges prevent leveraging HBF for high-throughput inference. First, Flash suffers from inherently high access latency (Boukhobza et al., 2025), which can hurt the end-to-end latency. Second, although HBF provides high peak bandwidth, it requires a high degree of parallelism to reach the peak bandwidth. Inefficient data layout can limit parallel access opportunities and result in low bandwidth utilization. Third, integrating HBF introduces heterogeneous memory resources, raising the challenge of managing these resources and exposing efficient abstractions to software.

Addressing these challenges requires hardware–software co-design. FlashAccel addresses these challenges through co-design across architecture, data layout, and system software. Architecturally, FlashAccel mitigates Flash access latency with SRAM buffers distributed across HBF dies for data prefetching. It also integrates HBF, HBM, and GPU cores into a unified accelerator to relieve the capacity bottleneck. At the data layout level, FlashAccel addresses the low bandwidth utilization challenge of HBF by designing specialized layouts for weights and KV cache, enabling high parallelism during inference. At the system level, FlashAccel provides an HBF-aware storage management layer to organize persistent data in HBF and a programming model that allows applications to efficiently utilize heterogeneous memory resources.

In summary, we make the following contributions.

  • •

    We identify the key challenges of employing HBF for LLM inference, including high access latency that affects the end-to-end latency, the gap between peak read bandwidth and effective bandwidth under LLM workloads, and the lack of management for heterogeneous memory resources.

  • •

    We introduce FlashAccel, an HBF-based accelerator for high-throughput LLM serving. FlashAccel combines hardware–software co-design techniques that hide high access latency, enable near-peak bandwidth for weights and KV cache, and efficiently manage heterogeneous resources.

  • •

    Experimental results show that FlashAccel significantly improves throughput and energy efficiency by 2.54×\times and 1.93×\times, respectively, compared with HBM-only GPU implementations.

2. Background & Motivation

2.1. LLM Workload

LLMs consist of multiple stacked transformer layers (Vaswani et al., 2017), each requiring storage for static model weights (shared across all requests) and dynamic KV cache (isolated per request) (Vaswani et al., 2017). LLM inference consists of prefill and decode phases with distinct computational characteristics (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023). Prefill processes all input tokens together, making it predominantly compute-bound. In decode, each request provides one token per step, leading to frequent access to the model weights and KV cache, which makes it memory-bound.

As KV cache grows over inference steps, most frameworks (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024) adopt PagedAttention-style mechanisms (Kwon et al., 2023) that partition KV cache into fixed-size blocks for fine-grained memory allocation, reducing fragmentation and improving memory utilization. Frameworks also manage KV cache eviction. Upon request completion, the computed KV cache is retained in memory for potential reuse by future requests. When memory is exhausted, the framework evicts history KV cache to serve new requests.

2.2. Memory Capacity Bottleneck

The rapid growth of model weights and KV cache has made GPUs’ HBM capacity a fundamental bottleneck for LLM inference. This bottleneck directly limits the batch size in the decode phase. Consider running Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) on an H100 GPU (NVIDIA Corporation, 2022) with 80GB HBM. After reserving approximately 64GB for model weights, only 16GB remains available for KV cache. For an 8K context length, each request requires about 2GB KV cache, meaning the GPU can support a batch size of at most 8. According to the Roofline model (Williams et al., 2009), larger batch sizes increase the arithmetic intensity of weight-related operations and thus improve GPU utilization. Figure 2(a) shows that a small batch size limits throughput, whereas larger batch sizes significantly improve throughput with only marginal impact on latency.

HBM capacity further limits the reuse opportunities of KV cache. Figure 2(b) illustrates the reuse opportunity in multi-turn interactions. KV cache generated in previous turns can be reused during the prefill phase for future turns, avoiding recomputation of this KV cache. However, reuse requires retaining KV caches in memory. In the example above, each request requires 2GB of KV cache, meaning a single GPU can store KV caches for only eight requests. When serving more requests, KV caches are frequently evicted, leading to low cache hit rates and additional recomputation overhead. Prior work (Wang et al., 2025a) shows that achieving high reuse efficiency may require up to 4×\times more memory capacity for KV cache.

Current LLM inference systems mitigate memory capacity limitations by interconnecting multiple GPUs, at the expense of increased deployment cost and system complexity (Sun et al., 2018). The aggravated inter-GPU communication significantly impacts performance, with collective communication accounting for up to 20% of total latency (Gond et al., 2025). In addition, system reliability degrades as scale increases. (Kokolis et al., 2025) reveals that in a 1024-GPU system, failures occur on average every 7.9 hours.

2.3. Flash for LLM Inference

Flash memory is attractive for alleviating the capacity bottleneck due to its high storage density. As shown in Figure 3(a), a Flash die comprises an array die stacked over a circuit die via hybrid bonding (Zhou et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025a). The array die stores data using vertically stacked NAND cells, while the circuit die integrates peripheral circuits. Figure 3(b) shows the Flash hierarchy of channel-die-plane-block-page. A Flash device consists of multiple channels, each of which serves as an independent interface and is shared by one or more dies. Each die contains multiple planes with independent read/write circuits in the circuit die, enabling parallel data exchange between the NAND array and the page buffer. Within a plane, blocks are the units of erase operation, while pages are the units of read and program operations.

Recent works such as AiF (Lee et al., 2025b), Lincoln (Sun et al., 2025), and Cambricon-LLM (Yu et al., 2024) use Flash for LLM inference. They store model weights in Flash and place compute units within Flash to exploit plane-level parallelism. These designs enable edge inference, but are not suitable for high-throughput inference. These designs provide only hundreds of GB/s bandwidth and few TFLOPS of computational capacity, far below modern GPUs. These limitations in both bandwidth and compute capacity directly restrict inference throughput. Moreover, they store only model weights in Flash but ignore the large KV cache footprint.

A more promising approach to accelerating LLM inference with Flash is to integrate a Flash device of high bandwidth with the GPU, alleviating its capacity bottleneck. The key to achieving high bandwidth is exploiting plane-level parallelism. An HBF can be realized by increasing the number of planes per die (e.g., partitioning a die into 16 planes (SanDisk, 2025)), adopting HBM-like 3D stacking (Jun et al., 2017) to enable parallelism across multiple Flash dies, and leveraging TSVs to provide high-bandwidth interconnects between Flash and GPUs.

The main concern with storing KV cache in Flash is endurance. For example, single-level cell (SLC) Flash typically provides about 100K P/E cycles (Mohan et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016; KIOXIA Corporation, 2022). Prior works (Sun et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2024) avoid storing frequently updated KV caches in Flash to circumvent endurance limits. However, recent advances in attention mechanisms make storing KV cache in Flash feasible. According to the DeepSeek report (DeepSeek-AI, 2025), the prefill cluster (approximately 764 GPUs) writes 266 billion new tokens per day 11 1 The prefill cluster processes 608 billion tokens in total, but 342 billion tokens are served via KV cache hits and do not require additional writes.. Building upon these inputs, the decode cluster (approximately 1,051 GPUs) generates an additional 168 billion tokens. Based on these statistics, each GPU in the prefill cluster writes 22.7TB of KV cache per day, while each GPU in the decode cluster writes 26.9TB of KV cache per day. SLC Flash can provide about 55 P/E cycles per day over a 5-year lifetime. Thus, a 1TB HBF device can sustain about 55TB of data writes per day, which is sufficient for the inference workloads. In addition, relaxing retention guarantees can extend endurance by up to 50×\times (Luo et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2012), making Flash a practical medium for KV cache storage.

3. Challenges

3.1. High Access Latency

Compared with HBM, Flash exhibits significantly higher access latency. Even with high read bandwidth comparable to HBM, the high read latency of HBF severely degrades end-to-end performance. Using HBF, the GPU receives the first batch of data roughly 4 μ​s\mu s (tR) after issuing an access request (Kouchi et al., 2020), whereas HBM requires only about 100 n​sns (Huang et al., 2021), which is a 40×\times gap. For example, a 4k ×\times 4k FP8 GEMV operation can be completed on H200 in approximately 4 μ​s\mu s. When using HBF instead, it incurs an additional 4 μ​s\mu s access latency, leading to a 50% end-to-end latency increase.

3.2. Low Bandwidth Utilization

Due to the inherent high read latency, Flash exhibits low per-plane bandwidth (e.g., a plane reads a 4KB page in 4 μ​s\mu s, 1 GB/s). Achieving high aggregate bandwidth requires exploiting parallelism across thousands of planes. For example, matching the 4.8 TB/s bandwidth of H200 requires 4,916 planes to read concurrently.

We define a hyper page as a logical access unit that aggregates one page from every plane. Accessing multiple hyper pages sequentially can maximize inter-plane parallelism and approach the peak bandwidth. When accessing data in HBF, we define plane load as the number of pages that need to be read from a plane. Since a plane serves page reads serially, the overall read latency is determined by the maximum plane load across all planes. If data is unevenly distributed across planes, some planes become idle earlier while others continue reading, reducing plane-level parallelism and bandwidth utilization. The resulting bandwidth loss directly prolongs memory-bound decode.

This issue is particularly evident in weight access. For an HBF of 4.8 TB/s bandwidth, its hyper page size is about 19MB. However, Figure 4(a) shows that a weight matrix in Qwen3-235B is only 12MB. As a result, accessing a single weight tensor activates only a subset of planes, leading to insufficient parallelism and bandwidth utilization. Although accessing multiple weight tensors consecutively increases data size beyond a hyper page, its benefit still strongly depends on data layout. Existing inference frameworks usually store weights in the order of variable initialization in the source code, rather than the order they are actually accessed during inference. In case ① of Figure 4(b), when weights A, B, and C are accessed consecutively, the source-code declaration order places D between A and B, yielding a maximum plane load of 3. In contrast, case ② of Figure 4(b) achieves a maximum plane load of 2. Therefore, reorganizing weights by execution order reduces the maximum plane load by 33% and correspondingly lowers access latency.

The problem is even more complicated for KV cache because its data layout changes at runtime. At each inference step, the system accesses a unified KV cache constructed from the KV caches of all active requests. Since active requests change over steps, even if the unified KV cache is evenly distributed across planes at one step, the balance does not persist. As requests complete and new ones arrive, the KV cache distribution becomes imbalanced in subsequent steps. As shown in Figure 5, requests 1–4 are processed in the first step, and their KV cache is evenly distributed across planes22 2 For clarity, we assume the size of each KV block in KV cache is the same as the page size of the plane in figures.. In a later step, if requests 1 and 3 complete, only requests 2 and 4 remain active. The unified KV cache becomes imbalanced across planes, yielding a maximum plane load of 3 versus an average load of 2, resulting in a 33% bandwidth loss. This imbalance becomes worse over time. Due to the paging mechanism and eviction process, the KV cache of a single request becomes fragmented across multiple planes. Meanwhile, the active request set at each step evolves in a near-random manner, resulting in an imbalanced distribution of unified KV cache across planes. Assuming each partitioned KV block of the unified KV cache is uniformly assigned to planes, the load can be modeled as a balls-into-bins problem (Raab and Steger, 1998; Sitaraman, 2001). Under this model, distributing 100GB KV cache of Qwen3-235B across 4,916 planes causes the maximum plane load to exceed the average load by 52%, leading to 52% bandwidth loss. Furthermore, existing attention kernels parallelize across requests, resulting in simultaneous reads of all requests’ KV cache. This strategy fails to align accesses at hyper-page granularity. As shown in Figure 5, attention kernels may simultaneously access two requests’ KV cache in the same plane, leading to contention analogous to bank conflicts, which further degrades bandwidth utilization.

3.3. System Resource Management

The third challenge is system-level support for HBF. Unlike HBM, HBF is non-volatile, so the system must support persistent data organization inside HBF for objects such as model weights and KV cache. It also has to coordinate HBF, HBM, and SRAM during execution. Existing approaches do not fit the management of HBF well. Using an HBM-style paging mechanism for data stored in HBF provides direct and low-latency access, but it does not support persistence, because page table mappings are discarded when the program terminates. Conventional Flash stacks support persistence but incur metadata and latency overhead from layered address translation (Agrawal et al., 2008; Boukhobza et al., 2025). Moreover, as HBF bandwidth approaches that of HBM, treating Flash as a lower tier behind HBM becomes increasingly inefficient because it forces unnecessary staging through HBM. Instead, HBF should be exposed as a directly accessible resource for GPUs, while SRAM is used to hide Flash access latency. This requires a storage management layer for persistent data in HBF and a programming abstraction for accessing heterogeneous memory resources.

4. Hardware Design

FlashAccel combines HBF, HBM, and GPU cores into a heterogeneous accelerator for LLM inference. FlashAccel can be realized using either co-located integration (CLI) (SanDisk, 2025) or cascaded integration (CSI) (Ha et al., 2026), as illustrated in Figure 6(a). CLI places HBF alongside the GPU, partially replacing HBM to increase overall capacity and lower HBM cost. CSI connects HBF to the GPU in a daisy-chain manner through the HBM base die, preserving more HBM stacks and thereby maximizing HBM capacity and bandwidth. In this heterogeneous memory system, HBM and HBF serve complementary roles. HBM handles small, frequently updated intermediate data for its low access latency, while HBF stores large, read-dominated data such as model weights and KV cache. Figure 6(b) shows the HBF stack architecture. Each stack contains 8 Flash dies above a base die, interconnected by TSVs. Each Flash die integrates an array die and a circuit die through hybrid bonding. Following (Sun et al., 2025) and (SanDisk, 2025), FlashAccel increases plane-level parallelism by scaling each Flash die to 96 planes. Figure 6(c) shows that HBF integrates SRAM buffers in different dies as caches for data prefetch to mitigate Flash latency. According to (Sun et al., 2025), the circuit die contains substantial unused silicon area. FlashAccel places SRAM in this unused area, providing each plane with an SRAM cache. For the base die, in addition to the NAND controller and PHY, we also integrate SRAM cache, increasing the overall SRAM capacity. Each stack has a total SRAM capacity greater than 2×P​e​a​k​_​B​a​n​d​w​i​d​t​h×R​e​a​d​_​L​a​t​e​n​c​y2\times Peak\_Bandwidth\times Read\_Latency to support the Flash data prefetch mechanism described in Section 6.2.3, ensuring the basic double-buffered pipeline. We target SLC-based HBF for its lower read latency and higher write endurance. Although SLC Flash provides lower bit density than multi-level cell (MLC) and triple-level cell (TLC), HBF still retains a substantial capacity advantage over HBM.

5. Data Layout Design

Data layout design is the core of FlashAccel co-design, because achieving high HBF bandwidth utilization depends not only on hardware capability, but also on whether data accesses can be arranged to match Flash parallelism. Efficient data layout enables data accesses in HBF to approach peak bandwidth.

5.1. Weights in HBF

To expose HBF parallelism, FlashAccel places static weights across all planes in execution order, balancing load and approaching peak bandwidth. Figure 7 illustrates the weight layout strategy. For a given model architecture, the computation graph of each inference step is fixed, which enables offline determination of the execution order. FlashAccel partitions each operator’s static weights into page-sized units (e.g., A0, A1, and A2) and maps them across all planes and channels in round-robin order. After mapping the current operator, the system continues with subsequent operators according to the execution order, starting from the plane immediately following the last assigned plane of the current operator. As a result, the entire weight set is approximately balanced across planes from a global perspective. Combined with the prefetch mechanism described in Section 6.2.3, which loads these weights sequentially, this data layout enables high HBF bandwidth utilization.

5.2. KV Cache in HBF

The layout of the KV cache is more complicated than that of static weights because the active request set changes at every inference step. FlashAccel organizes per-request KV blocks as a unified KV cache. This abstraction enables write, offload, and read policies that balance plane load and preserve HBF bandwidth.

At the beginning of a decode step, the unified KV cache can be divided into two types of KV blocks. Resident KV blocks are already stored in HBF from previous steps and have not been evicted. Nonresident KV blocks must be written into HBF from a remote KV cache pool or from newly generated prefill outputs produced on prefill GPUs. As shown in Figure 8 ❶, FlashAccel aggregates nonresident KV blocks into as many full hyper pages as possible and writes them to HBF to improve inter-plane balance. Residual blocks that do not fill a hyper page are placed randomly to avoid hotspots. Balancing incoming writes is insufficient because resident KV blocks may already be skewed across planes. This imbalance reduces bandwidth utilization in the memory-bound decode phase. To address this issue, FlashAccel rebalances plane load after the write phase through selective offloading. We first compute the average plane load of the unified KV cache and then offload excess pages from overloaded planes to HBM until no plane exceeds the average load (Figure 8 ❷). Benefiting from HBM’s low read latency, the offloaded data can effectively utilize HBM bandwidth. This selective offloading avoids extra HBF writes and thereby preserves Flash endurance. Since the same unified KV cache is typically reused across multiple subsequent decoding steps, the extra offloading overhead can be amortized.

During attention computation, conventional kernels load KV cache in parallel across requests. This may trigger concurrent reads to different requests whose KV blocks happen to reside in the same plane, causing plane conflicts that reduce parallelism. Figure 8 ❸ illustrates the proposed HBF-friendly loading scheme. The GPU performs accesses to HBF at hyper-page granularity to maximize effective bandwidth, and then processes all KV blocks within each hyper page in parallel. A small fraction of KV blocks offloaded to HBM is fetched from HBM in the same step. Using FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022), we compute partial attention results per KV block and then reduce them by request to obtain the final result.

Each decode step also produces new KV cache for every request. We temporarily buffer them in HBM (Figure 8 ❹). At the end of each step, once the filled blocks are sufficient to form one or more full hyper pages, we flush them back to HBF using the same hyper-page-based write policy (Figure 8 ❺). Since the KV cache generated at each decode step is too small to form a hyper page, directly flushing it to HBF would underutilize bandwidth. The proposed strategy avoids inefficiency and improves bandwidth utilization for KV cache writes and future reads.

Besides the above strategies, increasing the KV block size, i.e., storing more tokens in every KV block, can further mitigate inter-plane load imbalance. Under random plane mapping, increasing the KV block size significantly reduces the maximum plane load, as shown in Figure 9. A larger KV block spans multiple NAND pages and is therefore distributed across a group of adjacent planes rather than confined to a single plane. This spreads load over multiple planes, weakens local hotspots and reduces the amount of rebalancing required.

However, the KV block size cannot be arbitrarily large. Since a KV block is typically written to HBF only after it is filled, a larger block size leaves more partially filled data buffered in HBM and increases HBM pressure. For the Qwen3-235B model, a KV block size of 512KB with batch size 256 requires at least 8GB of HBM, imposing high HBM pressure on the CLI architecture. Larger block sizes also increase internal fragmentation. FlashAccel uses 256KB KV blocks to balance plane-level skew and HBM pressure.

6. System Design

The above data layout and access optimizations require system support at two levels. First, the system has to coordinate HBM, HBF, and SRAM during inference. Second, it must organize persistent data stored in HBF. Accordingly, FlashAccel provides a programming model for heterogeneous resource coordination and an HBF-aware storage management layer for persistent data organization. The programming model exposes a unified virtual address space to programs, while the storage management layer maintains the metadata needed to locate persistent objects in HBF.

6.1. HBF-aware Storage Management

FlashAccel uses a lightweight HBF-aware storage layer for persistent data placement. It treats model weights and per-request KV cache as persistent objects, partitions them into data units, and maintains per-object indexing metadata to locate them. In conventional Flash storage stacks, locating data typically requires two levels of indirection. The program first uses file-system metadata to obtain a logical address, which is then translated by the Flash translation layer (FTL) in hardware (e.g., SSD controller) into a physical Flash address. Since Flash does not support in-place updates, the two-level indirection is necessary. When data is modified, the new data must be written to a different physical address, and the FTL is responsible for tracking these remapped addresses. However, the FTL is costly for HBF, as it demands a GB-scale logical-to-physical mapping table (Gupta et al., 2009) stored in low latency SRAM or DRAM, and incurs extra address translation overhead (Agrawal et al., 2008). Our key observation is that both model weights and KV cache follow append-only write patterns. FlashAccel therefore eliminates the FTL and directly records the physical address of each data unit in the object’s indexing metadata. As a result, locating data in HBF requires only the indexing metadata, avoiding the overheads of FTL. By storing the metadata in Flash, we ensure data persistence. To match the block-level erase semantics of Flash, the storage layer adopts an isolated block allocation policy. Weight objects and each request’s KV cache object are placed in separate blocks. Because KV cache eviction occurs at request granularity, erasing the KV cache of one request does not affect weight objects or the KV cache objects of other requests, thereby avoiding write amplification and reducing Flash wear (Cai et al., 2017).

6.2. Programming Model

FlashAccel exposes HBF through a programming model comprising an interface set and a runtime. After the program invokes these interfaces, the runtime maintains page table mappings from logical addresses to the physical addresses of HBM, HBF, or SRAM. This design exposes heterogeneous memory through a unified virtual address space. The programming model provides different interfaces for accessing weights and KV cache stored in HBF, accounting for distinct access characteristics. To address the HBF access latency challenge, it also provides interfaces that leverage SRAM to hide data access latency.

6.2.1. Weight Access Interface

Weights are the simplest object in the model because they are static and read-only. FlashAccel introduces a primitive NandMmap interface to expose weight objects stored in HBF to the virtual address space. NandMmap maps a weight object in HBF into the virtual address space and returns a logical base address. The program can subsequently access the mapped weights using ordinary load operations on the returned logical address. Upon a NandMmap call, the runtime first reserves a contiguous free range in the virtual address space, as shown in Figure 10(a). It then retrieves the metadata of the target object from the storage management layer to obtain the physical page addresses of the mapped data in HBF. Finally, it updates the page table to associate the returned logical address range with the corresponding physical addresses in HBF. Since weights are static, these mappings can be established once during model initialization and reused throughout inference.

6.2.2. KV Cache Access Interface

Unlike model weights, the KV cache is maintained separately for each request rather than shared across requests. FlashAccel stores each request’s KV cache as an independent persistent object in the HBF storage management layer. However, during each inference step, the system must jointly read and write the KV caches of all active requests. To support this access pattern, we introduce a group object abstraction. GroupCreate logically combines the KV-cache objects of active requests in the same inference step into a single group object. Based on this abstraction, FlashAccel introduces three interfaces: GroupMmap, GroupWrite, and GroupArrange, to support grouped reads, append-only writes, and offloading, respectively.

GroupMmap maps a group object into a contiguous logical address space and returns the base address and a read table. The runtime first reserves a contiguous virtual address region, and then builds a plane-distribution table (Figure 11) for all objects in the group and uses it to pack data from different objects into hyper pages whenever possible. These hyper pages are mapped contiguously into the virtual region at hyper-page granularity. The runtime also returns the read table to resolve each offset of the logical base address to its corresponding object identifier. This design allows the program to access the group object through one logical address range, while transparently serving HBF accesses at hyper-page granularity for high bandwidth utilization.

GroupArrange performs the offloading mechanism described in Section 5.2. The runtime computes the load of the group object across different planes and derives the average load. It then migrates data from overloaded planes in HBF to HBM. Finally, it updates the page table so that the physical addresses of the offloaded data point to their new addresses in HBM (Figure 11). This interface alleviates load imbalance across planes and improves overall read bandwidth.

GroupWrite handles append-only writes to the KV cache, flushing data from HBM to Flash. GroupWrite takes a pointer to data in HBM together with a write table that specifies which object each portion of the data belongs to. Following the write policy described in Section 5.2, the runtime splits data in HBM into hyper pages whenever possible and distributes them across HBF in a plane-balanced manner. For data smaller than a hyper page, the runtime randomly selects planes for placement. The runtime updates the object metadata in the storage management layer, the page table, and the read table of GroupMmap according to the write table and the plane addresses determined during placement, so that the newly written data remains accessible.

6.2.3. Data Prefetch

FlashAccel incorporate a data prefetch mechanism into the programming model to leverage the SRAM resources to hide the high read latency of Flash. Specifically, FlashAccel introduces SramPrefetch, which takes a logical address (e.g., the returned address of NandMmap and GroupMmap for weights and KV cache, respectively) referring to data in HBF and a prefetch size as input, and returns an output logical address referring to prefetched data in SRAM for subsequent accesses. FlashAccel also provides SramRelease to release the allocated SRAM space after the last consumer finishes. A kernel therefore follows a simple pattern: prefetch to SRAM, compute on the returned address, and release the SRAM resources. For data objects larger than the SRAM capacity, the runtime split them into multiple smaller tiles that fit in SRAM and execute them sequentially. Figure 12(a) illustrates how a large weight matrix is split into three tiles, each of which is prefetched into SRAM, multiplied with the activation, and discarded before processing the next tile.

To overlap prefetch with computation, the runtime employs prefetch-aware scheduling. Figure 12(b) shows how SramPrefetch operations are extracted from the compute graph, organized into a queue following the topological order of the computational graph, and executed asynchronously from the compute kernels. This design allows Flash access latency to be overlapped with computation, as depicted in Figure 12(c).

When the runtime encounters a prefetch request, it first creates page table mappings for the returned logical address and initially points them to the original Flash addresses, ensuring that the data remains accessible. The runtime then attempts to migrate data in Flash to SRAM in the background at the hyper-page granularity. It first tries to allocate space in the SRAM of the plane. If that fails, it falls back to the SRAM on the base die. When allocation succeeds, the data is read from Flash into SRAM and the corresponding mappings in the page table are updated to the SRAM location. Otherwise, if no SRAM space is available, the original Flash mapping is retained. Figure 10(b) shows the page table after prefetching weights data from HBF.

SramPrefetch does not stall the execution of dependent compute kernels. If a compute kernel begins execution before data prefetch completes, the unprefetched portions retain their original Flash addresses in the page table, allowing the kernel to access the correct data. After the last consumer compute kernel completes, SramRelease reclaims the associated SRAM space for future prefetches.

7. Evaluation

7.1. Evaluation Setup

Workloads: Table 1 summarizes the four representative models used in our evaluation. These models cover popular attention mechanisms including group-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), multi-head latent attention (MLA) (Shao et al., 2024), and feed-forward network (FFN) variants, including dense FFNs and mixture-of-experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017) FFNs. We apply different parallelism strategies for these models including tensor parallelism (TP), data parallelism (DP) and expert parallelism (EP). FP16 is used for all models, except that the weights of DeepSeekV3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) are in FP8. We set two sequence length configurations for different workloads. For long-context workloads, we derive the average sequence lengths of all tasks in the LongProc benchmark (Ye et al., 2025), setting the input and output sequence lengths to 8.11K and 2.53K, respectively. The second configuration targets agentic workloads with multi-turn interactions. Based on statistics reported in (Wang et al., 2025b), we set the average input and output sequence lengths to 15K and 6K, respectively.

Baseline and Configuration: The baseline is a DGX-H200 node (NVIDIA Corporation, 2024). A DGX-H200 node contains 8 H200 GPUs within the same NVLink domain, each with 900 GB/s NVLink bandwidth. Each H200 GPU is equipped with 6 HBM3e stacks (Micron Technology, 2024), delivering a total of 141GB DRAM capacity and 4.8 TB/s memory bandwidth. This baseline configuration is denoted as 8×\timesH200.

We model an HBF stack designed to deliver HBM3e-level bandwidth while providing 8×\times higher capacity. Table 2 summarizes its configuration. Following Lincoln (Sun et al., 2025), we design the Flash die based on XL-Flash (Kouchi et al., 2020). Each Flash die contains 96 planes, and each plane has a capacity of 256MB. We derive area parameters from the die-shot in (Kouchi et al., 2020). For a conservative evaluation, tRt_{R} and tP​r​o​gt_{Prog} are kept the same as in (Kouchi et al., 2020) even though the capacity of each plane is reduced by 4×\times. We integrate HBF into the GPU and evaluate two FlashAccel configurations: CSI and CLI. CSI places 6 HBF stacks alongside the 6 HBM stacks in H200. Since FlashAccel does not require large HBM capacity for data storage, each HBM stack is reduced to 2 DRAM layers to minimize cost in CSI design. CLI replaces 5 of 6 HBM stacks with HBF and retains 1 HBM stack. Since HBF offers higher capacity, fewer GPUs are needed to store model weights. Therefore, beyond 8×\timesCSI and 8×\timesCLI configurations, we also evaluate 4×\timesCSI and 4×\timesCLI.

Simulation: We build an event-driven simulator on top of LLMCompass (Zhang et al., 2024) to model the latency of LLM inference on both FlashAccel and conventional GPUs. LLMCompass searches tiling strategies to find efficient GEMM mappings on GPU hardware and uses ScaleSim (Samajdar et al., 2018) to estimate latency. We extend it with a NAND simulator that models page access latency at plane granularity. We modify the memory model of LLMCompass to simulate the access of data residing in Flash and SRAM cache by providing the corresponding latencies.

7.2. Evaluation Results

Figure 13 shows the throughput per GPU in the decode phase across five hardware configurations under varying models and sequence lengths. We use two decode latency service-level objectives (SLOs)  (Zhong et al., 2024), 50ms (∼\sim20 tokens/s/user) and 100ms (∼\sim10 tokens/s/user). FlashAccel removes the capacity bottleneck of HBM on batching, shifting the limiting factor for throughput from memory capacity to latency budget. Since larger batch sizes increase the arithmetic intensity of memory-bound FFN operations, this shift directly improves decode throughput. For each configuration, we therefore use the largest batch size that satisfies both the SLO and HBM capacity constraints, and report throughput per GPU normalized to the baseline. For example, for LLaMA3.1-405B with 15K/6K context length, each request requires 10GB of KV cache, limiting the maximum batch size of 8×\timesH200 to 30, whereas under a 50ms SLO, 8×\timesCSI can support a theoretical batch size of 110 after accounting for the memory footprint of model weights.

Across all models, sequence lengths, and SLOs, 8×\timesCSI consistently outperforms the baseline, delivering a 2.15×\times average throughput gain by supporting substantially larger batch sizes. 8×\timesCLI shows lower throughput than 8×\timesCSI, as the CLI architecture has only 5 HBF stacks, resulting in 16.7% lower bandwidth compared to CSI. Under the strict 50ms SLO, this bandwidth limitation causes it to slightly underperform the baseline on DeepSeek-V3 model and Qwen3-235B model. Under a 100ms SLO, CLI can load more KV cache per step, enabling larger batch sizes and a 2.04×\times overall throughput improvement.

We further investigate configurations with fewer GPUs. For HBM-based GPUs, a 4×\timesH200 setup cannot fit model weights and is not evaluated. Both 4×\timesCLI and 4×\timesCSI suffer from reduced aggregate bandwidth. For LLaMA3.1-405B and Qwen3-Coder-480B, loading weights alone takes close to 50ms, leaving insufficient time for KV cache loading and computation under a 50ms SLO. Thus, these models cannot be served under this constraint. For other models, the limited bandwidth and strict SLO restrict batch size, resulting in lower throughput than the 8×\timesH200 baseline. When the SLO is relaxed to 100ms, more KV cache can be loaded per step, enabling larger batch sizes. Despite using fewer GPUs, FlashAccel still outperforms the baseline on LLaMA-405B, Qwen3-235B, and Qwen3-480B in throughput per GPU.

Figure 14 shows throughput per GPU when scaling to 16 GPUs. For HBM-based GPUs, the additional memory capacity allows larger batch sizes. However, scaling to 16 GPUs moves communication from NVLink to RDMA (NVIDIA Corporation, 2024), reducing bandwidth by about 9×\times and making all-to-all communication in EP much more expensive. As a result, the baseline shows little throughput improvement, and in some cases even degrades. Although 16×\timesCSI and 16×\timesCLI still achieve higher throughput per GPU than 16×\timesH200, their performance is also limited by communication overhead. Compared with 8×\timesCSI and 8×\timesCLI, both show lower throughput per GPU. We also find that, for both CSI and CLI, an 8×\times HBF-based GPU system delivers higher throughput per GPU than a 16×\times HBM-based GPU system. Because each HBF-based GPU provides more capacity, a smaller system within a high interconnect bandwidth domain can sustain the workload, improving both cost efficiency and throughput per GPU.

7.3. Ablation Study

We ablate each optimization in FlashAccel. Figure 15 presents the latency breakdown of 6 accelerator configurations executing a Qwen3-235B model with a batch size of 256. Plain HBF denotes an HBF-based GPU without any optimizations. We further construct three ablated variants by disabling an optimization from the full CSI FlashAccel design at a time, namely prefetching, weight layout, and KV cache layout. With all optimizations enabled, FlashAccel matches HBM-based latency within ∼\sim4%, including 2% offloading overhead. Figure 15 reports throughput under a 100ms SLO. Disabling prefetching, weight layout, and KV cache layout degrades throughput by 55%, 7%, and 15%, respectively, relative to FlashAccel. Plain HBF suffers a 65% throughput loss and falls below the HBM-based GPU. Overall, these results show that all three optimizations are necessary to close the performance gap of HBF. Prefetching plays a dominant role in mitigating access latency, while layout optimizations further improve bandwidth utilization.

7.4. Write Issues

Flash suffers from write-side limitations in both bandwidth and endurance. Table 2 shows that the write latency of program operation (tP​r​o​gt_{Prog}) is significantly higher than the latency of read (tRt_{R}), which limits HBF write bandwidth. While the read bandwidth reaches 4.6 TB/s for CSI, the peak write bandwidth is only 245.8 GB/s. The endurance is another concern. Prior works (Luo et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2012) demonstrate that reducing retention time from 3 years to 3 days can extend P/E cycles by up to 50×\times. Conservatively, we assume that reducing the retention time can extend the endurance by up to 10×\times, increasing the P/E cycles from 100K to 1M. Even so, it still cannot match the nearly unlimited write endurance of DRAM. However, the wide adoption of new attention mechanisms, like GQA and MLA, reduces write volume compared to multi-head attention (MHA), making it possible to store KV cache in Flash. Across all evaluated configurations, each HBF-based GPU generates and writes at most 276MB of new KV cache per second in the decode node (8×\timesCSI running Qwen3-480B under a 100ms SLO, 1138 tokens/s). In addition, based on the input/output length ratio (i.e., ∼\sim2.58:1) in agent workloads (Wang et al., 2025b), each HBF-based GPU writes another 712MB of KV cache per second from the prefill node. In total, each HBF-based GPU writes 988MB of KV cache per second, taking only 3.9ms and incurring an additional overhead of 4%. Over a 5-year deployment period, this amounts to 148,570TB of total KV cache writes. With 1152GB capacity and 1M P/E cycles, CSI provides 1,125,000 TBW, sufficient for KV cache storage.

7.5. Prefill and KV Cache Reuse

During the prefill phase, each request usually contains enough tokens to achieve high compute intensity, even without constructing a large batch size. In this case, both HBM-based GPUs and HBF-based GPUs can process the prefill requests efficiently. In multi-turn interactions, however, the GPU for prefill needs to store the KV cache of previous turns for each session for future turns in the same session to reuse it, avoiding the recomputation for these cached tokens. Larger capacity allows the system to reduces KV cache eviction. Figure 16 reports the KV cache hit rate measured using multi-turn interaction traces (badlogic, 2026) on different numbers of HBM-based GPUs and HBF-based GPUs. Due to the large memory capacity, both 8×\timesCLI and 8×\timesCSI can store the KV cache for all sessions and achieve the ideal hit rate. In comparison, even when we scale the HBM-based GPU system to 16 GPUs, its hit rate is still 50% lower than that of the HBF-based GPU system. Figure 16 also shows that the higher hit rates of 8×\timesCSI and 8×\timesCLI reduce the number of tokens that require computation by up to 89% compared with 8×\timesH200, thereby providing additional speedup.

7.6. Energy and Area Analysis

Flash memory suffers from high read energy consumption. While hybrid bonding can reduce read power, measurements from a real hybrid-bonded Flash prototype still show a read energy of 8 pJ/bit (Yanagidaira et al., 2025b), which is 2.7×\times higher than that of HBM3e (2.99 pJ/bit (Antepara et al., 2025)). After integrating HBF, the overall TDP of CSI and CLI architectures increases 1.31×\times and 1.23×\times, respectively. Nevertheless, thanks to the throughput advantages of HBF, we observe improvements in tokens per Joule. Figure 17 illustrates the energy efficiency (tokens/J) of different accelerators under a 100ms SLO. On average, 8×\timesCSI and 8×\timesCLI deliver 1.93×\times and 1.66×\times higher energy efficiency than 8×\timesH200, respectively.

Our evaluation shows that HBF occupies an area of 149mm2, which is 1.23×\times larger than that of standard HBM3e (121mm2). This overhead stems from our conservative assumptions based on the design in (Kouchi et al., 2020), which uses only 96 wordline layers. Recent technologies (Cho et al., 2025; Thimmaiah et al., 2026; Yanagidaira et al., 2025a) have achieved over 300 wordline layers, significantly improving storage density and reducing area overhead for a given capacity. Using array dies with more wordline layers allows HBF to achieve area parity with the HBM stack. Even with only 96 wordline layers, our HBF design still achieves 6.5×\times higher density than HBM3e.

8. Related Works

Flash Offloading Strategy: Prior works (Sheng et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025; Alizadeh et al., 2024; Gugger et al., 2022) offload model weights or KV cache to SSDs to mitigate the DRAM capacity bottleneck, enabling LLM execution without out-of-memory failures. However, these designs are fundamentally constrained by the low SSD bandwidth, leading to extremely high decode latency, which limits their practicality in datacenter deployment. FlashAccel addresses this issue by increasing plane-level parallelism in Flash and employing dedicated layout optimizations to achieve high bandwidth.

In-storage Processing Accelerators: These accelerators (Lee et al., 2025b; Sun et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024) place compute units inside Flash to exploit its internal bandwidth for on-device inference. However, the limited silicon area inside Flash restricts computational capacity, resulting in low throughput. Moreover, they do not support storing KV cache in Flash, leaving capacity challenges unaddressed. FlashAccel instead integrates HBF with GPUs to provide high computational capacity, and enables KV cache storage via SLC Flash and system support for append-only KV cache writes.

Processing-in-memory Accelerators: Some works (Park et al., 2024; Heo et al., 2024; Seo et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025) accelerate attention execution using DRAM-based processing-in-memory (PIM) which provides high internal bandwidth but limited computational capacity. They mainly target MHA that has low arithmetic intensity. Recent MLA and GQA impose higher computational demands that are difficult for PIM to sustain. In addition, PIM does not address the inherent low density of DRAM which leads to high cost. By contrast, FlashAccel improves density with Flash and, through GPU integration, supports attention mechanisms requiring more computation.

9. Conclusion

This work points out the key obstacles that prevent HBF from translating its capacity advantages into LLM-serving performance, and addresses them through co-design across architecture, data layout, and system software. FlashAccel introduces an SRAM cache at the architectural level and a prefetch interface at the system level to mitigate the high access latency of Flash. A specialized data layout fully leverages plane-level parallelism for weights and KV cache to improve bandwidth utilization. An HBF management layer and a programming model address the management and usage of heterogeneous memory resources. Experimental results show that FlashAccel achieves 2.54×\times higher throughput than HBM-based GPU.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
